content:
# 1 Maccabees Chapter 14 — Disagreement Log

**Date:** 2026-03-17 | **Verses:** 49 | **Disagreements:** 36

---

## Summary
The encomium poem (vv.4-15) generates the most significant structural disagreement: all translators recognize it as poetry and format it accordingly, but LOGOS separates it formally with a header while EMET renders it as prose. Vocabulary disagreements concentrate on political and legal terminology in the inscription (vv.27-48).

---

## Disagreements

**v.4** — Poetry formatting: EMET renders vv.4-15 as unbroken prose; LOGOS, PNEUMA, and SOPHIA format them as indented parallelistic poetry with lineation. SOPHIA ruling: format as verse from v.5-15 (v.4 is transitional prose).

**v.5** — "took Joppa as a harbor" — all agree; "opened access to the islands of the sea" (LOGOS) vs. "made a way to the islands of the sea" (EMET/SOPHIA) vs. "opened the gate to the islands of the sea" (PNEUMA)

**v.7** — "gathered many captives" (EMET/SOPHIA) vs. "brought home many captives" (PNEUMA) — PNEUMA adds "home" for emotional resonance.

**v.8** — "the land gave its produce" (EMET/LOGOS/SOPHIA) vs. "the earth gave back its harvest" (PNEUMA)
- "trees of the plain" — all agree; "plain" vs. "fields" question; SOPHIA: "plain" preferred per Greek πεδίον.

**v.9** — "Old men sat in the streets" — all agree; the echo of Zech 8:4 is preserved in all translations.
- "glorious and warlike apparel" (EMET/SOPHIA) vs. "glorious and martial dress" (LOGOS) vs. "military glory" (PNEUMA condenses)

**v.10** — "furnished them with the means of defense" (EMET/LOGOS/SOPHIA) vs. "made them strong" (PNEUMA)
- "to the end of the earth" (EMET/SOPHIA) vs. "to the ends of the earth" (LOGOS/PNEUMA) — number of "end."

**v.11** — "Israel rejoiced with great joy" — all agree.

**v.12** — "under his vine and under his fig tree" — all four agree exactly; key biblical allusion preserved universally.
- "none to make them afraid" — all agree.

**v.14** — "all the poor of his people" (EMET) vs. "all the humble of his people" (LOGOS/SOPHIA) vs. "the poor of his people" (PNEUMA) — Greek: ταπεινοὺς; "humble" preferred over "poor" as more precise to the Greek sense.
- "sought out the law" — all agree.
- "removed every lawless and wicked man" (EMET) vs. "exterminated every lawless and wicked man" (LOGOS) vs. "hunted down every lawbreaker and scoundrel" (PNEUMA) vs. "removed every lawless and wicked person" (SOPHIA)

**v.15** — "multiplied the sacred vessels" (EMET/LOGOS/SOPHIA) vs. "filled it with sacred vessels" (PNEUMA)

**v.18** — "wrote to him on bronze tablets" — all agree on this detail of the Spartan communication.

**v.20** — Spartan letter salutation: "The rulers and the city of the Spartans" — all four agree on this unusual formulation.
- "Simon the great priest" — all agree; this is the Spartan way of addressing him.

**v.21** — "about your glory and honor" (EMET/SOPHIA) vs. "about your glory and honor" (LOGOS) vs. "your glory and honor" (PNEUMA) — minor.

**v.24** — "a great gold shield weighing a thousand minas" (LOGOS/SOPHIA) vs. "a great gold shield weighing a thousand minas" (EMET) — agreement. PNEUMA: "a massive golden shield."
- 1000 minas ≈ 571 kg; an extraordinary diplomatic gift.

**v.25** — "What thanks shall we give to Simon and his sons?" (EMET/SOPHIA) vs. "How shall we thank Simon and his sons?" (LOGOS/PNEUMA)

**v.27** — Date: PNEUMA converts "one hundred and seventy-second year" to "140 BCE"; others preserve regnal year.
- "Asaramel" — all preserve the untranslated toponym/title.

**v.29** — "of the family of Joarib" (EMET/SOPHIA) vs. "of the house of Joarib" (LOGOS/PNEUMA)
- "exposed themselves to danger" (LOGOS/SOPHIA) vs. "put themselves in danger" (EMET/PNEUMA)

**v.30** — "was gathered to his people" — all four agree; classical biblical idiom.

**v.32** — "spent much of his own money" — all agree.
- "armed the men of valor" (EMET) vs. "armed the warriors" (LOGOS/SOPHIA) vs. "armed the nation's warriors" (PNEUMA)

**v.33** — "where formerly the weapons of the enemies had been" (EMET) vs. "where the arms of the enemy had been stored before" (LOGOS) vs. "previously an enemy weapons cache" (PNEUMA) vs. "where formerly the weapons of the enemy had been stored" (SOPHIA)

**v.35** — "his rule and his glory" (v.4, EMET) vs. "his authority and renown" (LOGOS) vs. "his leadership and in his glory" (PNEUMA) — back to v.4 reference.

**v.36** — "those who were in the city of David in Jerusalem who had built themselves a citadel" — all agree on structure; PNEUMA: "The men in the Davidic citadel."
- "defile all the surroundings of the sanctuary" (EMET) vs. "defile the precincts of the sanctuary" (LOGOS/SOPHIA) vs. "a constant source of pollution and harassment" (PNEUMA)

**v.38** — "On account of this" (EMET) vs. "On account of these things" (LOGOS/SOPHIA) vs. "For all this" (PNEUMA)

**v.41** — "until there should arise a faithful prophet" — all four translate this crucial caveat identically.

**v.42** — "take charge of the sanctuary and that he should appoint officers" (EMET) vs. "be responsible for the sanctuary and appoint officers" (LOGOS) — LOGOS preferred for clarity.

**v.43** — "clothed in purple and wear gold" (EMET) vs. "clothed in purple and wear a gold ornament" (LOGOS/SOPHIA) vs. "wear purple and the gold ornament" (PNEUMA) — SOPHIA: "gold ornament" in v.43.

**v.44** — "gold buckle" (EMET) vs. "gold clasp" (LOGOS/SOPHIA/PNEUMA) — consistent with earlier ruling.

**v.46** — "ethnarch" — all four preserve the Greek title. Agreement.
- "pleased to be high priest and to be general and ethnarch" (EMET) vs. "pleased to serve as high priest, commander, and ethnarch" (LOGOS/SOPHIA) vs. "agreeing to serve as high priest, commander, and ethnarch" (PNEUMA)

**v.48** — "so that Simon and his sons might have them" — all four agree on this final phrase.
